If `123456` was literal, that was only a placeholder—sorry that wasn’t explicit. But even a real code may expire during this upload.

The reliable immediate fix is a short-lived granular npm token:

1. On npmjs.com, create a granular token restricted to `keating`, with:

   - Package permission: Read and write
   - Bypass 2FA: enabled
   - Short expiration

2. Use it temporarily without putting it in shell history:

```bash
KEATING_NPMRC_PATH="$(mktemp)"
chmod 600 "$KEATING_NPMRC_PATH"

read -rsp "Temporary npm token: " KEATING_NPM_TOKEN
printf '\n'
printf '//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken=%s\n' "$KEATING_NPM_TOKEN" > "$KEATING_NPMRC_PATH"

NPM_CONFIG_USERCONFIG="$KEATING_NPMRC_PATH" \
NODE_OPTIONS=--tls-max-v1.2 \
nix shell nixpkgs#nodejs_22 -c npm publish \
  --access public \
  --fetch-retries=10 \
  --fetch-retry-mintimeout=1000 \
  --fetch-retry-maxtimeout=5000

rm -f "$KEATING_NPMRC_PATH"
unset KEATING_NPM_TOKEN KEATING_NPMRC_PATH
```

No OTP is required when that token has “Bypass 2FA” enabled. If TLS still exhausts all ten attempts, switch network paths—such as temporarily disabling VPN or using a hotspot—and rerun.

Longer-term, the release workflow should use [npm trusted publishing/OIDC](https://docs.npmjs.com/trusted-publishers/) so releases don’t depend on expiring OTPs or long-lived secrets.
